agent_answer.notes: All 20 corpus papers (S001-S020) directly compare a retrieval-augmented generation condition against a no-retrieval/closed-book condition on a factual benchmark and state a conclusion about whether retrieval improves factual accuracy. The papers disagree, so the answer to the question is mixed/conditional: RAG does not universally improve factual accuracy; its effect depends on the model, benchmark and query type. Distribution: 7 papers find RAG improves accuracy (S002, S006, S008, S011, S016, S017, S018); 8 find no measurable change (S003, S004, S005, S007, S009, S015, S019, S020); 4 find RAG decreases accuracy (S001, S012, S013, S014). Note on internal inconsistencies in two papers: S020's own results table shows RAG 64.6% vs no-retrieval 52.3%, yet its abstract/conclusion states no measurable improvement; S009's table shows lower RAG accuracy on both datasets, yet its conclusion states no measurable improvement. In both cases the paper's own stated conclusion was used for classification. Claims recorded: claim-000001 through claim-000041.

answer_text: Retrieval-augmented generation does not universally improve factual accuracy; its effect depends on the model, benchmark, and query type. The corpus presents mixed evidence: 7 papers (S002, S006, S008, S011, S016, S017, S018) report that RAG improves factual accuracy or reduces hallucination, 8 papers (S003, S004, S005, S007, S009, S015, S019, S020) report no measurable change, and 4 papers (S001, S012, S013, S014) report that RAG decreases factual accuracy or increases hallucination.
